introduction_markdown: CAMEROON GENERAL CERTIFICATE OF EDUCATION BOARD, General Certificate of Education Examination. 0760 HISTORY 1, ADVANCED LEVEL, JUNE 2020. Multiple choice question paper. Time allowed: one and a half hours (1h 30 minutes). Instructions to candidates: use a soft HB pencil. Answer ALL the 50 questions in this examination. All questions carry equal marks. Each question has FOUR suggested answers: A, B, C and D. Decide which answer is appropriate and mark only one answer for each question (if more than one answer is marked, the question scores zero). Avoid spending too much time on any one question: move on and come back to it later. Mobile phones are NOT allowed in the examination room.
incertitudes: Sujet scanné sans couche texte, lu en image. La page de garde indique bien « 0760 HISTORY 1 », « JUNE 2020 », « ADVANCED LEVEL », « MULTIPLE CHOICE QUESTION PAPER », une heure et demie ; 50 questions, aucune figure ni carte.

Défaut d'impression : le pied de page des pages 2 à 5 porte la référence « 2016/0760/1/C/MCQ » alors que la page de garde porte « 4-/0760/1/C/MCQ » et « © 2020 CGCEB » (probable réutilisation de la maquette de 2016). Le sujet est bien celui de juin 2020 d'après la page de garde.

Aucun corrigé officiel n'est fourni : toutes les clés sont déduites de l'historiographie usuelle (manuels camerounais d'histoire, programme du GCE) et n'ont pas pu être confrontées à un barème officiel. Les points ne sont pas imprimés (toutes les questions comptent à égalité).

Dix QCM ont été convertis en questions ouvertes parce que deux options sont défendables ou que l'énoncé est discutable : 4 (obstacle principal de la Baptist Missionary Society), 7 (Alliés en 1914-1916 : désaccord stratégique ou attaques désorganisées), 12 (facteur principal du nationalisme au Southern Cameroons), 14 (première réaction organisée contre le plébiscite de l'ONU : parti cité de mémoire, détail non vérifié), 16 (UC dominante en 1965 : opposition écrasée ou ralliée), 24 (facteur économique : Révolution industrielle, matières premières ou marchés), 27 (question EXCEPT où les quatre options sont des griefs plausibles), 32 (néocolonialisme : franc CFA ou exploitation continue), 33 (renversement d'Amin : plusieurs causes), 46 (première grande réussite de maintien de la paix : Congo ou Suez). La réponse visée figure dans le corrigé, avec la mise en garde.

QCM conservés avec une clé défendable mais moins sûre : 15 (le poste de Prime Minister de West Cameroon après la Constitution fédérale de 1961 ; la Chambre des chefs du Southern Cameroons était antérieure), 17 (révocation de Ngom Jua en 1968 : motif général du dessein unitaire de Ahidjo, motifs exacts discutés), 18 (« Self-Reliance » retenu comme principe qui ne figure pas dans la politique étrangère d'Ahidjo : non-alignement, bon voisinage et coopération sont les principes habituellement cités), 22 (CMS considérée comme la première société missionnaire d'Afrique de l'Ouest parmi les options ; les missions catholiques portugaises plus anciennes ne sont pas une « société » au sens des autres options), 29 (WWII retenue comme facteur principal après 1945 plutôt que les partis), 36 (Bill of Rights : limiter les prérogatives royales plutôt qu'empêcher le retour de Jacques II), 39 (Bismarck : « isoler la France » retenu, « protéger l'Empire contre une attaque française » est proche), 48 (chute de Khrouchtchev retenue comme seule option cohérente ; sa part causale est discutée).

Détails historiques énoncés avec prudence dans les corrigés et non vérifiables ici faute de source : Q1 (rôle de la mort de Gawolbe dans les migrations des Bali-Chamba ; pas de date ni de nom de successeur donnés), Q3 (relief des monts Mandara et cavalerie peule), Q6 (recrutement forcé dans l'intérieur), Q10 (dissolution de l'UPC et de l'USCC en juillet 1955), Q13 (Endeley « Leader of Government Business » en 1954, Premier en 1958), Q20 (Bakassi : arrêt de la CIJ en 2002, accord de Greentree en 2006). Aucune statistique ni citation inventée.

Écarts typographiques du sujet imprimé, recopiés avec de légers ajustements : Q25 option B « Niger Detta » corrigé en « Niger Delta » ; Q40 option A « Francis Ferdinand » conservé tel qu'imprimé (le corrigé écrit Franz Ferdinand, comme la question 41) ; Q38 « theTroppau » séparé en « the Troppau » ; Q2 option D « there was the absence of lacked powerful lineage heads » conservée telle qu'imprimée (phrase agrammaticale) ; Q13 option A « CNF » recopiée telle quelle ; Q42 imprime « 1919-1923 » pour la conférence de Paris (la conférence elle-même date de 1919-1920). Q30 option D « settles » imprimé pour « settlers » (écrit settlers). Filigranes et publicités (gcerevision.com, application « kawlo ») ignorés.
Converties en questions ouvertes par le relecteur (clé ou options discutables) : 4, 7, 12, 14, 16, 24, 27, 32, 33, 46.

questions.enonce_markdown: The death of Gawolbe in the 1830s influenced the migration of:
questions.corrige_markdown: Gawolbe was a Chamba leader from the Chamba country of the Adamawa region. His death in the 1830s was followed by a succession crisis and by pressure from the Fulani, and groups of Chamba (the ancestors of the Bali-Chamba) moved south-west into the Bamenda Grassfields, where they eventually settled in Bali-Nyonga and founded other Bali chiefdoms. The Bamileke, the Bafut and the Gbaya are different peoples whose settlement is not linked with the death of Gawolbe. **Answer: A.**
themes: pre-colonial peoples and states of cameroon

questions.enonce_markdown: A distinct characteristic of the Kom and Aghem fondoms of the grassland region in the 19th century was that:
questions.corrige_markdown: Kom and Aghem were organised fondoms ruled by a Fon, so they were not stateless (C is wrong), and they were governed through lineage heads and regulatory societies (D is wrong). What set them apart from most Grassfield societies, such as Bamum and Bafut, which followed the father's line, was that succession and inheritance passed through the mother's line, that is, matrilineal succession. **Answer: B.**
themes: pre-colonial peoples and states of cameroon

choix.texte: there was the absence of lacked powerful lineage heads.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main reason for the failure of the Jihad in Mandara land before 1847 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Fulani jihad in the Adamawa-Mandara region relied on cavalry. The Mandara (Wandala) kingdom lay in and around the rugged Mandara mountains, where horses could not manoeuvre, so the mounted Fulani warriors could not break the defenders, who resisted from the hills. The relief of the land was therefore the main reason for the failure. Distance from Yola, Adama's health and Fulani disunity are, at most, minor factors. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: lack of unity of the Fulani.

questions.enonce_markdown:
A major contributor to the limited success of The London Baptist Missionary Society in Cameroon between 1841 and 1884 was:

*Options as printed:* A) harsh tropical climate and diseases.   B) transport and communication difficulties.   C) man power shortages and disagreement.   D) clash with indigenous culture.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Baptist missionaries (Joseph Merrick, Alfred Saker and their colleagues) worked on the coast of Cameroon after 1841. Several obstacles slowed their work: tropical diseases and the climate killed or disabled many missionaries and discouraged recruits, there was a shortage of staff and money, travel by sea and river was slow, and some local customs conflicted with Christian teaching. Because more than one of the printed options was a genuine obstacle, the question has no single unambiguous key. The obstacle most often stressed for this period is the heavy toll of tropical diseases.

**Intended answer: A (harsh tropical climate and diseases).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The strongest reason for British reluctance to annex Cameroon in spite of the demand for it in the 1870s was because:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the 1870s the Duala chiefs (for example King Bell and King Akwa) asked Britain to take over their territory, but London refused. British merchants and the Consul already controlled the coastal trade in palm oil and other products, so Britain enjoyed the commercial benefits without the expense of administering a colony. The strongest reason was therefore her satisfaction with her trade dominance. Fear of antagonising Germany belongs to the 1880s, and disease or interest in East Africa were not the decisive reasons for refusal. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: she did not want to antagonize Germany.
she was afraid of the harsh tropical diseases.
she was more interested in East Africa.
she was contented with her trade dominance of the area.

questions.enonce_markdown: While establishing plantations along the Cameroon coast, the Germans encountered the greatest difficulty in the domain of:
questions.corrige_markdown: German plantations (cocoa, banana, rubber, palm) on the coast and around Mount Cameroon needed many workers, but the local coastal population was small and unwilling to work for low wages when it could farm or trade on its own account. The shortage of labour was the greatest difficulty and led the administration to use forced recruitment from the interior. Transport, capital and health care were also problems, but none was as persistent as labour. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Allied inability to swiftly conquer the Germans during the First World War in Cameroon can be attributed to:

*Options as printed:* A) Allied disagreement over war strategy.   B) disorganised Allied attacks of German forces.   C) German use of reserved forces in Kamerun.   D) absence of indigenous support to the Germans.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The conquest of Kamerun (1914-1916) took much longer than expected. The British, French and Belgian forces operated from different directions, with separate commands, and their commanders disagreed about strategy and objectives, so their attacks were poorly co-ordinated. The Germans also used the rainforest, the climate and a retreat towards Spanish Muni (Rio Muni). Options A and B describe the same weakness (lack of co-ordination among the Allies) in different words, so the question has no unique key. The wording that best names the cause is disagreement over strategy.

**Intended answer: A (Allied disagreement over war strategy).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The administering powers of Cameroon between 1922 and 1946 were:
questions.corrige_markdown: After the defeat of Germany in the First World War, Kamerun was partitioned between Britain and France, and the League of Nations confirmed the two mandates in 1922. They lasted until 1946, when the territories became United Nations Trust Territories under the same two administering powers. Belgium administered Ruanda-Urundi, not Cameroon, and Germany had lost its colonies. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A common factor that provoked the Baya, Duala and Bamum revolts against French rule during the Mandate era was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The French mandate administration relied on forced labour (the indigenat and compulsory recruitment for roads, railways, plantations and public works). The Baya rising of 1928-1931 was linked to forced recruitment for railway construction and to forced collection of produce. Bamum and Duala protests in the same period also complained about forced labour. Land expropriation (B) was mainly a Duala grievance, and cash-crop imposition (D) was not common to all three, so forced recruitment is the common factor. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: disrespect of indigenous authority and customs.
failure to return expropriated indigenous lands.
forceful recruitment of indigenes as labourers.
forceful imposition of cash crop cultivation.

questions.enonce_markdown: The immediate consequence of the May 1955 UPC uprising in French Cameroon was that:
questions.corrige_markdown: The UPC-led riots of May 1955 were put down by the French authorities, and in July 1955 a decree dissolved the UPC and its allied organisations (including the USCC trade union), forcing the leaders underground. An amnesty came later (1957), the Loi Cadre was passed in France in 1956, and Um Nyobe was killed in September 1958. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: partial amnesty was granted to UPC fighters.
the UPC and USCC were banned.

questions.enonce_markdown: An important event which took place in French Cameroon in February 1958 was the:
questions.corrige_markdown: Semi-autonomy (the 1957 statute), the Legislative Assembly (ALCAM, 1957) and Andre-Marie Mbida's appointment as Prime Minister (May 1957) all happened in 1957. In February 1958 Mbida's government fell and Ahmadou Ahidjo took over as head of government. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: granting of semi-autonomy to French Cameroon.
creation of the Legislative Assembly in Cameroon.
rise to power of Mbida as Prime Minister.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The most important factor that influenced the growth of nationalism in the British Southern Cameroons during the Trusteeship era was:

*Options as printed:* A) the role of political parties.   B) the activities of trade unions.   C) the hatred for Ibo domination.   D) the activities of ex-servicemen.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Several factors fed nationalism in the British Southern Cameroons: political parties (KNC, KPP, KNDP), trade unions, ex-servicemen and the UN Trusteeship system. Many accounts stress resentment of Nigerian, and especially Igbo, domination of jobs and commerce in the Southern Cameroons as the underlying grievance which pushed people to demand a separate political future. Because the question asks for the 'most important' factor and parties, unions and ex-servicemen were also channels of the same feeling, the key is open to debate.

**Intended answer: C (the hatred for Ibo domination).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Dr E.M.L. Endeley's popularity reached its peak in British Southern Cameroons in 1954 when he:
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1954 the Lyttelton Constitution gave the Southern Cameroons a separate status, no longer part of the Eastern Region of Nigeria, with its own House of Assembly. Endeley, whose KNC won the election, became Leader of Government Business, the highest office in the territory at that time, which marked the peak of his popularity. The title of Premier or Prime Minister came later (1958), and the policy of Benevolent Neutrality is associated with the end of the 1950s. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: became the leader of the CNF.
championed the policy of Benevolent Neutrality.
became the leader of Government Business.
became the Prime Minister of the territory.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The first organised reaction against the UN Plebiscite in the British Southern Cameroons came from:

*Options as printed:* A) CUC of S.T. Muna.   B) KNDP of J.N. Foncha.   C) CIP led by Manga William.   D) KNC led by Endeley.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The UN decided in 1959 that the Southern Cameroons would vote in a plebiscite with only two alternatives, joining Nigeria or joining the Republic of Cameroon, and independence was not offered. Small groups that wanted independence protested; the Cameroons Indigenous Party (CIP) of Manga William is the party named in the course notes as the first organised protest. The KNDP and the KNC took part in the plebiscite campaign on the two alternatives and did not reject it. This detail is hard to check in the sources available, so the key is uncertain.

**Intended answer: C (CIP led by Manga William).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: An important aftermath of the 1961 Federal Constitution on the State of West Cameroon was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Under the 1961 Federal Constitution each federated state had its own legislature and government headed by a Prime Minister. In West Cameroon the head of government, previously called Premier, became Prime Minister (Foncha first held it while also serving as Vice-President of the Federation). The House of Chiefs already existed in the Southern Cameroons, and West Cameroon obtained only a few federal ministerial posts. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the decrease in the number of seats in the West Cameroon House of Assembly.
the creation of the West Cameroon House of Chiefs.
the creation of the post of Prime Minister.
many ministerial positions for West Cameroon in the Federal Government.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Ahidjo's UC emerged as the dominant party in East Cameroon by 1965 because:

*Options as printed:* A) he had crushed all opposition parties.   B) he had the support of the opposition parties.   C) the opposition leaders went into exile.   D) he had the support of John Ngu Foncha.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In East Cameroon the Union Camerounaise gained the upper hand in the early 1960s: opposition leaders were arrested or restricted, but many opposition parties also rallied to the UC or merged into a UC-led grouping, which prepared the single party (CNU) created in 1966. Option A is too absolute ('all'), and exile (C) concerned the UPC rather than all opposition leaders. The question mixes repression and absorption, so the key is uncertain.

**Intended answer: B (he had the support of the opposition parties).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most appropriate reason for the dismissal of Augustine Ngom Jua in 1968 as Prime Minister of West Cameroon was because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Ahidjo's aim after 1961 was to centralise power and replace the federation with a unitary state (achieved in 1972). Ngom Jua, a strong-willed Prime Minister of West Cameroon with his own political base, was seen as an obstacle to that design and was dismissed in 1968. Options B and C describe aspects of his position, but D is the most general and appropriate reason. The exact motives of Ahidjo are debated. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: he was against the promotion of bilingualism.
he was against the creation of the one party state.
he advocated the autonomy of West Cameroon.
he was a threat to Ahidjo's design for a unitary state.

questions.enonce_markdown: Cameroon's foreign policy objective under President Ahmadou Ahidjo was based on all the following principles EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: Ahidjo's foreign policy was presented as one of good neighbourliness, international co-operation and non-alignment, together with African unity. Although Cameroon was in practice close to France, Self-Reliance was not a declared principle of its foreign policy in the way the other three were (Cameroon depended heavily on French aid and cooperation). So the principle that does NOT belong is D. **Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Paul Biya's ascension to power was greeted with euphoria in 1982 because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Paul Biya succeeded Ahidjo in November 1982 and promised a new style of government: reform, rigour and moral renewal, and better days for the population (the 'New Deal'). That hope explains the enthusiasm. The other options (dislike of Ahidjo's foreign policy, hatred of Ahidjo, personal looks) are not supported as the reason for the welcome. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: of the hatred for Ahidjo's foreign policy.
he promised reforms and better days ahead.

questions.enonce_markdown: President Paul Biya's greatest success in international affairs was when he:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Bakassi dispute with Nigeria threatened war in the 1990s. Cameroon took it to the International Court of Justice, whose judgment (2002) awarded the peninsula to Cameroon, and the Greentree Agreement (2006) organised a peaceful handover. This peaceful settlement is regarded as Biya's greatest diplomatic achievement. Relations with China and Francophonie membership date from earlier periods, and hosting a summit is a lesser achievement. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: secured Cameroon's admission into the Francophonie.
hosted the OAU Summit in Yaounde.
peacefully resolved the Bakassi Crisis with Nigeria.

questions.enonce_markdown: The greatest effort made at ending the slave trade on the coast of West Africa was:
questions.corrige_markdown: After Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807, it created the West Africa Squadron of the Royal Navy (from 1808), which patrolled the coast, arrested slave ships and freed captives, mainly at Freetown. Treaties with African rulers, the right to search ships and compensation were all useful tools, but the naval patrol was the biggest and most sustained effort. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The first Christian missionary body to be implanted in West Africa was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Of the societies listed, the Church Missionary Society (CMS) was the first to start work in West Africa, in Sierra Leone in the first years of the 19th century. The Methodist and Glasgow societies followed later, and the Catholic missions of the Society of African Missions arrived later still. Earlier Catholic missions of the Portuguese period were not conducted by a society of this type. **Answer: A.**
themes: christian missionary activity in west africa

questions.enonce_markdown: The largest theocratic state in West Africa was created by:
questions.corrige_markdown: The jihad launched by Usman dan Fodio in 1804 among the Hausa states created the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest Islamic theocratic state of West Africa, governed according to Islamic law through emirs under the Sultan of Sokoto. Seku Ahmadu's Macina state and El-Hajj Omar's empire were smaller, and El Kanemi of Bornu defended an existing state against the Fulani. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Usman Dan Fodio in Northern Nigeria.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The most important economic factor that triggered the scramble for Africa was:

*Options as printed:* A) the desire to acquire raw materials.   B) the search for markets.   C) the impact of the Industrial Revolution.   D) the pressure mounted by European traders.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Industrial Revolution created factories that needed raw materials, markets for manufactured goods and outlets for capital. The desire for raw materials, the search for markets and pressure from traders all follow from it, so it is the root economic cause of the scramble. Because A and B are also standard economic causes, the choice of the 'most important' one is a matter of emphasis.

**Intended answer: C (the impact of the Industrial Revolution).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The immediate reason for the convening of the Berlin West Africa Conference in 1884 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Berlin West Africa Conference (November 1884 to February 1885) was hosted by Bismarck, the German Chancellor, after disputes over the mouth of the Congo and the Congo Basin (including the Anglo-Portuguese treaty of 1884 and the rival claims of King Leopold II, France and Portugal). Franco-German rivalry over Morocco belongs to the early 1900s. The Niger and Egypt were secondary issues at the conference. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: European scramble over the Congo Basin.
Anglo-French rivalries over Egypt and Sudan.

questions.enonce_markdown: Samori Toure of the Mandinka Empire resisted French occupation in the 1890s mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Samori Toure built a large empire in the upper Niger region (the Wassoulou empire) and fought the French for many years until his capture in 1898. His main motive was to defend the independence and sovereignty of his empire. He sought some foreign contacts, but he did not want annexation by Britain, and he could not count on firm British or African allies. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: he wanted British annexation of his empire.
he was sure of his military assistance from Britain
he was sure of the assistance from neighbouring African states.
he wanted to preserve the sovereignty of his empire.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The educated elite severely criticised the policy of Indirect Rule because of all of the following reasons EXCEPT:

*Options as printed:* A) it attached more importance to illiterate traditional rulers.   B) it was exploitative and did not promote meaningful development.   C) they were ignored in the policy.   D) they were not given white collar jobs.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The educated Africans (clerks, lawyers, teachers, journalists) opposed Indirect Rule because it handed authority to chiefs, often illiterate, instead of to them, because they were left out of the native authorities, and because it did little for development and was seen as exploiting the people. Options A, B and C are therefore all recognised criticisms. 'White collar jobs' were in fact mostly held by the educated in the colonial service, so D is the weakest as a criticism of the policy and is taken as the exception. The question is imperfect, since the educated also complained about limited promotion.

**Intended answer: D (they were not given white collar jobs).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: Africans participated in the Second World War in all the following ways EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: Africans took part in the war as soldiers and carriers, as labourers on war-time projects, as producers of raw materials and foodstuffs (rubber, tin, cocoa, palm products) and as donors to war funds. Conferences of the Axis powers (Germany, Italy and Japan) were not held in Africa, so this is the option that does not describe African participation. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: supply of labourers for different war-time projects.
provision of basic raw materials and foodstuffs to the belligerents.
donation of financial support to Allied War Fund.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main factor of African nationalism after 1945 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Second World War weakened Britain and France, taught thousands of African ex-servicemen new ideas and skills, spread the ideals of the Atlantic Charter, and encouraged the USA and the USSR to oppose colonial rule. It therefore created the conditions for the rise of mass nationalism, which political parties, trade unions and the press then organised and expressed. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: the role of the local press.
the effects of the Second World War.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main reason for the success of the National Liberation Front (FLN) in the Algerian War of Independence of 1954-1962 was because:
questions.corrige_markdown: The FLN began the armed struggle in November 1954 and won because it had the backing of most of the Algerian population, which supplied fighters, shelter and funds, and so could sustain a long guerrilla war that France could not win. De Gaulle's government fought the FLN before negotiating the Evian Accords (1962), and the French settlers opposed independence. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: it received massive support from the masses.
it had support from Charles de Gaulle's government.
European countries did not support France.

questions.enonce_markdown: A major repercussion of the prolonged liberation war in Angola was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Angolan war against Portuguese rule (1961-1974) ended after the 1974 coup in Portugal, and independence in 1975 was immediately followed by a civil war between the liberation movements (MPLA, FNLA and UNITA), in which the Cold War powers and South Africa intervened. The civil war is the major repercussion. Independence was the outcome of the war, and Portuguese repression took place during the war, not after. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the evacuation of white settlers from Angola.
the granting of independence to Angola.
the suppression of nationalist activities by Portugal.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The core negative economic impact of Neo-colonialism in French Equatorial Africa is:

*Options as printed:* A) the imposition of the Franc CFA as currency.   B) that loans are granted at high interest rates.   C) less French financing of development projects.   D) continuous exploitation and under-development.
questions.corrige_markdown:
After independence France kept strong economic links with its former colonies. The best-known mechanism of this control is the CFA franc, a currency issued under French guarantee and tied first to the French franc, which limits the monetary independence of the states. The wording 'continuous exploitation and under-development' (D) describes the general result and is also defensible, so the printed key is uncertain.

**Intended answer: A (the imposition of the Franc CFA as currency).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The central reason for the overthrow of Idi Amin of Uganda in April 1979 was that:

*Options as printed:* A) hatred for his repressive and authoritarian reign.   B) his hostile and unpopular foreign policy.   C) economic decline leading to rising unemployment.   D) the nationalisation of foreign investments.
questions.corrige_markdown:
Amin, who had seized power in 1971, ruled by terror, and his expulsion of the Asians (1972) and the economic collapse added to the opposition at home. He was overthrown in April 1979 by Tanzanian forces and Ugandan exiles after his troops had attacked Tanzania in 1978. Options A, B and C each contributed, and the question does not say which is 'central'. The intended answer is the repressive and authoritarian character of the regime.

**Intended answer: A (hatred for his repressive and authoritarian reign).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The prolonged survival of Apartheid in South Africa was due to the following reasons EXCEPT:
questions.corrige_markdown: Apartheid lasted from 1948 to the early 1990s partly because several Western powers (Britain, the USA and others) did not apply UN sanctions strictly, because South Africa had a strong army and economy, and because the black movements (ANC, PAC, Inkatha and others) were divided. The regime was not popular in Africa: it was condemned by the OAU and by most African states. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the fact that the regime was very popular in Africa.
failure by Western Powers to respect UN sanctions.
South Africa's military and economic strength.
disunity among the black resistant movements.

questions.enonce_markdown: A political cause of the frequent civil wars in Africa was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Many African civil wars, such as in Angola and the Congo, were fought between leaders and movements with opposed ideologies and ambitions, often backed by Cold War rivals. This is a political cause. Religious rivalry is a social cause, geography is physical, and multinational corporations are an economic factor. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: religious rivalries among the ethnic groups.
geographical diversities of the African states.

questions.enonce_markdown: The main reason why the British Parliament passed the Bill of Rights in 1689 was to:
questions.corrige_markdown: After the Glorious Revolution of 1688, Parliament offered the crown to William III and Mary II and imposed the Bill of Rights (1689). It forbade the monarch to suspend laws, to raise taxes or keep an army in peacetime without Parliament's consent, and it guaranteed regular parliaments, free elections and freedom of speech in Parliament. Its main purpose was to limit royal power. James II had already fled, and the Catholic exclusion was one clause, not the main aim. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: prevent James II from taking back the crown.

questions.enonce_markdown: Thomas Paine is credited in the history of the American Revolution of 1776 for:
questions.corrige_markdown: Thomas Paine's pamphlet Common Sense (January 1776) argued clearly and in simple language for independence from Britain and won many colonists over to it, which helped to unite them behind the Declaration of Independence in July 1776. The Royalists were on the British side, protests against taxation began much earlier (Stamp Act, 1765), and Paine did not found a nationalist movement. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: leading the Royalists in the war against Britain.
convincing the colonists not to pay British taxes.
uniting the colonists to declare independence.

questions.enonce_markdown: "... any European intervention in the affairs of Latin America will be considered as an unfriendly disposition to the USA." This was a concrete manifestation of:
questions.corrige_markdown: The statement paraphrases the Monroe Doctrine, announced by President James Monroe in 1823, which warned the European powers not to interfere in the newly independent states of the Americas. The Troppau Protocol (1820) and the Holy Alliance were European instruments for intervening against revolutions, and the Continental System was Napoleon's blockade against British trade. **Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The chief aim of Bismarck's foreign policy between 1871 and 1890 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: After defeating France in 1871 and taking Alsace-Lorraine, Bismarck expected French revenge. His whole alliance system (the Dreikaiserbund, the Dual Alliance with Austria, the Triple Alliance, the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia) aimed to keep France without allies. Securing Austria and Russia was a means, not the aim, and isolating Russia was the opposite of his policy. Option C states the purpose, and D the method. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: to secure the friendship of Austria and Russia.
to protect the German Empire from French attack.

questions.enonce_markdown: Britain entered the First World War on the side of the Entente Powers mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914 after German troops entered Belgium, whose neutrality Britain had guaranteed by the Treaty of London of 1839. The assassination of the Archduke (28 June 1914), the Austrian attack on Serbia and the German declaration of war on Russia started the crisis but did not by themselves bring Britain in. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The immediate cause of World War I was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The immediate cause was the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914. Militarism, the alliance system and colonial rivalries were long-term causes. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: the role of the alliance system.

questions.enonce_markdown: The greatest achievement of the Paris Peace Conference, 1919-1923 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The Paris Peace Conference (opened in January 1919) produced the Treaty of Versailles, which included the Covenant of the League of Nations, the first world organisation for peace. Disarmament was imposed only on the defeated powers, self-determination was applied unevenly (it was not given to colonial peoples), and the minority problems of Central and Eastern Europe were not solved. **Answer: A.**

choix.texte: formation of the League of Nations.

questions.enonce_markdown: Dr. Fridtjof Nansen was famous in the history of the League of Nations for:
questions.corrige_markdown: Fridtjof Nansen, the Norwegian explorer and diplomat, was the League's High Commissioner for Refugees. He organised the return of prisoners of war and the relief of refugees after the First World War and created the 'Nansen passport' for stateless people. Reparations were handled by other bodies, workers' conditions by the International Labour Organisation, and health by the League's Health Organisation. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: assisting refugee of World War I.

questions.enonce_markdown: The last step towards the collapse of Collective Security in the 1930s was:
questions.corrige_markdown: Collective security was weakened by the Japanese conquest of Manchuria (1931), the Italian attack on Abyssinia (1935), the remilitarisation of the Rhineland (1936), the Anschluss with Austria (1938) and the occupation of Czechoslovakia (1939). The last step was Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939, which made Britain and France go to war and ended the system. Pearl Harbour (1941) happened after the war had begun. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour.

questions.enonce_markdown: The most distressing impact of World War II on Germany was that:
questions.corrige_markdown: In 1945 Germany was occupied by the four Allied powers (the USA, Britain, France and the USSR), lost territory in the east, and was later divided into two states (1949), with Berlin also divided. This division and occupation was the most distressing consequence. The loss of colonies dates from the First World War, and disarmament and economic damage, although real, were less lasting. **Answer: D.**

choix.texte: she was disarmed by the Allies.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The pioneer major success of the UNO in its peacekeeping mission was:

*Options as printed:* A) preventing the occupation of South Korea.   B) halting the Israeli invasion of Egypt.   C) restoring the independence of Kuwait.   D) preventing the disintegration of Belgian Congo.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the Congo (1960-1964) the UN force ONUC was sent after independence from Belgium and the secession of Katanga, and it helped to keep the country united. Korea (1950) was a UN military action led by the USA, Suez (1956) was the first armed UN peacekeeping force (UNEF) after the Suez War, and Kuwait (1991) was a coalition authorised by the Security Council. Because B could also be argued as the 'pioneer' operation, the key is uncertain.

**Intended answer: D (preventing the disintegration of Belgian Congo).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The policy adopted by the Western Powers to prevent the expansion of Communism in Asia was known as:
questions.corrige_markdown: Containment, formulated by George Kennan and applied through the Truman Doctrine (1947), aimed to stop the spread of communism, including in Asia (Korea, Vietnam, SEATO). War Communism was Lenin's economic policy (1918-1921), Peaceful Co-existence was a Soviet policy of the 1950s, and Ostpolitik was West Germany's policy towards Eastern Europe. **Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A major consequence of the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 was:
questions.corrige_markdown: The crisis (October 1962) ended when the USSR withdrew its missiles from Cuba. Khrushchev was seen at home as having given way and was removed from power in 1964, partly for this reason. Russo-American relations improved afterwards (hotline, 1963 test-ban treaty), the Berlin Wall was built in 1961, and relations between the USSR and China worsened. **Answer: B.**

choix.texte: the fall of Nikita Khrushchev from power.
the construction of the Berlin Wall.

questions.enonce_markdown: Israel made the greatest territorial gains in the war against the Arab states during:
questions.corrige_markdown: In the Six-Day War of June 1967 Israel captured the Sinai Peninsula and the Gaza Strip from Egypt, the West Bank and East Jerusalem from Jordan, and the Golan Heights from Syria. In 1956 Israel occupied Sinai but withdrew in 1957, and the 1973 war did not bring lasting gains. **Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Relations between the USA and China improved in the 1970s mainly because:
questions.corrige_markdown: The USSR and China quarrelled in the 1960s, with border clashes in 1969. Both Washington and Beijing saw the advantage of closer relations against the Soviet Union, which led to President Nixon's visit to China in 1972. The USA did not support Chinese expansion, and China never gave up its claim over Taiwan. **Answer: C.**

choix.texte: of American support for Chinese expansion in Asia.
the Soviet condemnation of Nationalist China.
China's clash with the Soviet Union.
China gave up claims over Nationalist Taiwan.
